We are 404 Sun Not Found, a team from Kyrgyzstan exploring how interactive software can make space science easier to understand. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we built Lunar Landing Navigator to connect NASA data, 3D visualization, and hands-on exploration of lunar sunlight and Earth visibility.
summary:
Where on the Moon can you see the Sun and Earth—and for how long?

Lunar Landing Navigator turns NASA data into an interactive experience for exploring this question. Users can rotate a 3D Moon, change the date, compare locations, and descend to a human-height view of measured south-polar terrain. Connected timelines help users explore how sunlight and Earth visibility change and find continuous geometric visibility windows.

The prototype combines NASA/JPL SPICE astronomical geometry with LRO LOLA elevation data. Its distinctive feature is connecting numerical analysis with a surface perspective of the same location and time: users can investigate a condition on a chart, then explore what it looks like from the ground.

Built for students, educators, and curious explorers, the application makes lunar site-and-time trade-offs easier to understand. It clearly distinguishes geometric visibility, local terrain obstruction, and unknown terrain coverage. It is an educational prototype for preliminary exploration, not a tool for certifying landing safety or operational missions.
details:
Explore the Moon. Change the time. Understand the conditions.

Lunar Landing Navigator connects an interactive 3D Moon, measured terrain, and astronomical calculations in one browser application.

Try the application: https://fizeroo.github.io/lunar-landing-navigator/

Explore the code and documentation: https://github.com/Fizeroo/lunar-landing-navigator

The problem

Choosing a lunar location also means choosing a time. Sunlight and Earth visibility change, and nearby terrain can obstruct a direction that appears clear in a simpler geometric model.

For students and the public, these relationships can be difficult to understand through coordinates, tables, and separate datasets. Our project brings them together so users can explore how a change in location or date affects the conditions they see.

What users can do

  • Explore the Moon: rotate and zoom the globe, select coordinates, or choose a catalogue location.
  • Move through time: follow changing Sun and Earth directions across connected views.
  • Compare candidate locations: evaluate 25 points within a prepared south-polar region and inspect up to three alternatives.
  • Explore the surface: descend to approximately 1.7 metres above the modelled ground, look around, and walk within the supported terrain area.
  • Compare two sites: inspect visibility timelines, continuous intervals, and upcoming events.
  • Find time windows: search for continuous reference-horizon visibility intervals of a chosen duration and compare alternative start times.
  • Save scenarios: keep configurations locally for further exploration.

What makes the experience different

The numerical analysis and the surface experience describe the same selected place and time.

A user can examine a visibility interval, change the date, and then look toward the Sun or Earth from the lunar surface. This connects abstract geometry with a spatial experience that is easier to understand.

The application also makes uncertainty visible. It distinguishes a known local terrain obstruction from insufficient terrain coverage, rather than treating an unknown horizon as clear.

How NASA data powers the project

NASA/JPL SPICE — Where are the Sun and Earth?

Offline Python scripts use SpiceyPy and NASA/JPL SPICE kernels to prepare Sun and Earth vectors in a Moon-fixed frame. The available period runs from 1 October 2026 through 1 February 2027 UTC. The browser interpolates these prepared data, allowing interactive time changes without requesting an external astronomy service for every movement.

NASA LRO LOLA — What does the local terrain look like?

A measured elevation subset approximately eight kilometres across, with 80-metre grid spacing, supports the local terrain model and obstruction checks. Coarser elevation layers provide surrounding visual context without extending the scientific coverage of those checks.

NASA imagery — How is the scene presented?

NASA SVS lunar imagery, Deep Star Maps, and Blue Marble imagery provide visual context. These images are used for presentation; they are not live observations.

JPL Horizons — How are calculations checked?

Comparisons with JPL Horizons provide a related-model check of astronomical geometry. They are not independent observational validation.

Who benefits

Students and educators can use the application to explain lunar illumination, visibility, terrain, and time-dependent conditions through interactive examples.

The public can explore NASA datasets without installing specialist scientific software.

People exploring early mission concepts can compare simplified scenarios while seeing the assumptions and limits behind the results.

How we built it

The browser application uses TypeScript, Three.js, HTML, CSS, and Vite. Python tools, including SpiceyPy, NumPy, and Rasterio, prepare the scientific and terrain data offline. GitHub Actions builds the static application for GitHub Pages.

This approach combines responsive browser interaction with reproducible data preparation.

Scientific scope and limitations

Mission-window searches and visibility timelines use a smooth-sphere reference horizon. Local terrain obstruction checks are separate and have finite coverage. An unobstructed direction within the available terrain does not prove that the distant horizon is clear.

The terrain grid does not resolve individual rocks. Geometric sunlight visibility is not a calculation of electrical power, and geometric Earth visibility does not guarantee a working radio link.

The prototype does not model landing dynamics, eclipses, soil properties, or operational safety. It supports education and preliminary exploration.

Use of AI

Claude Code and OpenAI Codex assisted with development, review, testing, and documentation. The application does not use an AI model at runtime. Scientific values are derived from the documented source data.
